rv.q: Cookson's production is a tumultuous re-creation of Charlotte Brontë's novel.
This endlessly inventive, admirably kinetic production looks again at Charlotte Bronte's well-worn classic and remakes it as something fresh and exciting.

This is a production full of intelligent detail - from the use of multiple voices to deliver Jane’s agonised internal monologues to Melanie Marshall’s expressive, sung performance as Rochester’s mad wife, Bertha.
Although Sally Cookson’s production is full of wit, resource and invention, and went down a storm with the audience, watching it feels like speedreading a great book.
This is a fully compelling night at the theatre.
A rewarding, if long evening, trendily staged, celebrating one of the most popular novels of female empowerment ever written.
The whole ensemble come together in a beautifully choreographed set of scenes, perfectly timed and probably testament to a long period of gestation and rehearsal.

cn.t: Sally Cookson's inventive National Theatre production earns mostly strong notices, though some feel the condensed transfer loses detail from the Bristol original. Feminist in spirit and kinetically staged, it's bold reimagining slightly dulled by necessary cuts.
